title: The stain remains - Winnipeg Free Press
subtitle: Breaking News, Sports, Manitoba, Canada
article: This article was published 21/06/2008 (6280 days ago), so information in it may no longer be current.

MORE than three years ago, a young Winnipeg police officer shot Matthew Dumas twice, killing him. An inquest into the 2005 death wrapped up on Friday. An objective conclusion from all the evidence presented would find that the constable Mr. Dumas lunged at with a screwdriver had no option but to use lethal force.

Many of those witnesses thought or wished the angry young man had been subdued in other ways - some wondered why he wasn't tackled, one officer used his pepper spray. People heard the officers surrounding Mr. Dumas order him to put down his weapon, to halt his aggressive advances, warning that he would be shot. The testimony of an RCMP use-of-force expert indicated Const. Dennis Gburek followed correct procedure. If anything, he allowed Mr. Dumas to get too close before using his gun.

The family, represented at the inquest by a lawyer, likely is not satisfied. Mr. Dumas was stopped and detained by another officer who noticed he was hiding a weapon up his sleeve. The two fought and Mr. Dumas ran. The officer said he felt he couldn't risk trying to cuff the man. Many witnesses at the inquest said they wished he had, a sentiment likely shared by much of the public that has watched the painful dissection of yet another tragic encounter between police and an aboriginal man.

Matthew Dumas was innocent of the home invasion that sent police scurrying to track suspects, leading one officer to stop him. But beyond those facts, attempts to draw comparisons to the 1988 shooting death of aboriginal leader J.J. Harper would be specious. Except for this: J.J. Harper's death left an indelible stain on the relationship between Winnipeg police and native people in this city and that infected the Dumas affair. The Winnipeg Police Service has tried to repair the strained relations, dispel the ill will, but a serious analysis would concede that distrust dies hard.

The distrust is unlikely to abate until the Winnipeg police can present the investigations into shootings as irrefutably independent, which demands that they be conducted by an outside body, such as the RCMP. This would protect the interests of the officers involved and of the families of victims by protecting the evidence collected and the conclusions drawn from accusations of bias. Unlike the night that J.J. Harper died, Matthew Dumas was shot in full daylight, with witnesses to attest to the chain of events leading to the discharge of an officer's gun. But no police department should investigate its own. No matter how professionally the reviews are handled, they will naturally carry the suspicion they are an inside job.
